newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk Islamist outsider Erbakan draws secular ire.
newsitem.headline: Turk Islamist outsider Erbakan draws secular ire.

text.p: Turkey's first Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, who now faces a demand that his party should be outlawed, is a longtime political outsider who has drawn the ire of the country's secularist elite.
A prosecutor called on Wednesday for the constitutional court to outlaw Erbakan's Welfare Party on grounds that it threatens Moslem but secular Turkey's basic principles of state.

"It has become clear that (Welfare) has become a focus of actions contrary to the principle of secularism in the constitution and has pushed our country towards a civil war atmosphere," said charges read out by prosecutor Vural Savas.
Erbakan's unlikely coalition with conservatives has been locked in a bitter political war of attrition with secularists over his plans for Islamist reforms since he took office last June.

But the resolve shown in his chequered 28-year political journey to power, long obstructed by opposition from secularists and political rivals, suggests the veteran Welfare leader will rise to the latest challenge.

Erbakan capitalised on disarray in the right-wing political establishment to win a narrow victory in 1995 general elections. Personal rivalries across the political spectrum opened the way for his coalition with pro-Western Tansu Ciller, who had been Turkey's first woman prime minister.
Many voters were drawn by his promise of an economic revival and a raising of Turkey's international profile.
He repeatedly espoused a vision of global Moslem brotherhood, going against the grain of Turkey's decades-long ambitions to get closer to Europe and the United States.
"The West learned everything it knows from the Moslems," he said in a newspaper interview before coming to office.
Erbakan visited Iran and Libya shortly after taking power in trips that angered Turkey's Western allies, who regard the two countries as rogue states.
Statements made by Erbakan subsequently reinforced concerns about his stated hostility to NATO and the European Union.

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel nearly cancelled a visit to Ankara in March after Erbakan chided EU countries, saying they would "bow their heads when they talk with Turkey" about the cost of its customs union with the EU.
"The new world leader Turkey will receive the respect and treatment which it deserves," he told his party faithful.

But Erbakan has remained powerless to prevent a blossoming of defence links between Turkey and Israel, sought by the Turkish military, that has drawn anger from Welfare supporters as well as many in the Arab world and Iran.
His resilience has helped him withstand a constant stream of hostility from the secularist media, which he blames for unseating the government by targeting him with "false agendas".

The 70-year-old, who served as deputy prime minister in two coalition governments in the 1970s, managed on Tuesday to fight off the latest of a series of censure motions with a narrow margin in parliament.

His secularist coalition partners are seen as a major factor in preventing Erbakan from implementing the Islam-based theories he distilled during long years in opposition in a manifesto called the "Just Order".

Political and economic realities have undone manifesto vows to scrap interest rates, do away with "world imperialism and Zionism as well as Israel and a handful of champagne-drinking collaborators in the holding companies that feed it".

His plans to develop the Developing-Eight, an economic cooperation group of Moslem countries, have yet to get off the ground, while the domestic economy remains mired in deep public deficits and persistently high inflation.
Erbakan, a mechanical engineer, spent two years researching at a West German university and factories in the Ruhr during the post-war reconstruction boom after graduating at the age of 22.
His time abroad did not distract him from his obligations as a Moslem -- he has been praying five times a day since the age of 13 -- nor impress him with the ways of the West.

He was born in the northern town of Sinop in 1926, one of six children of a father who had served as a travelling Islamic judge in the crumbling Ottoman Empire at the beginning of the century. Erbakan is married with three children.

He entered politics as an independent Islamist MP for the conservative city of Konya in 1969, accusing then prime minister Suleyman Demirel, now president, of removing him as head of a respected business group because of his beliefs.
